Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Latin word

cum

cum (+ subjunctive)

conjunction, with the subjunctive

although, while; since, as; since (it is so long since); when; whenever; whereas, while; while, as (in past narrative)

In this lexicon

  • although

    also used · classical · Ov. Pont. 1.3.39–40: cum bene sit clausae caveā Pandīone nātae, nītitur in silvās illa redīre suās

  • since

    the recommended word · classical · Cic. Clu. 123: quae cum ita sint (Lewis & Short); Cic. Off. 1.54: quī cum ūnā domō jam capī nōn possint, in aliās domōs … exeunt

  • since

    also used · classical · Cic. Clu. 82: annī sunt octō cum ista causa in istā meditātiōne versātur (Lewis & Short); Plaut. Aul. prol. 4: hanc domum jam multōs annōs est quom possideō (Lewis & Short)

  • when

    the recommended word · classical · Ter. And. 309: Facile omnēs, cum valēmus, rēcta cōnsilia aegrōtīs damus.; Quint. 1.9.5: cum indoctum puerum vīdisset, paedagōgum ejus percussit

  • whenever

    also used · classical · Cic. Att. 1.6.2: tum dēnique cum illō vēnimus; Cic. Verr. 2.5.27: cum ad aliquod oppidum vēnerat, eādem lectīcā ūsque ad cubiculum dēferēbātur (Lewis & Short)

  • whereas

    the recommended word · classical · Cic. Sen. 17: cum aliī mālōs scandant, … ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī

  • while

    also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 5.97: Sōcratēn ferunt, cum ūsque ad vesperum contentius ambulāret …

  • cum … tum: both … and

    classical

  • cum maximē (tum maximē): just

    classical

  • cum … tum: not only … but also

    classical

  • dextram jungere cum aliquō: shake hands

    modern

  • cum aliquō tēlephōnicē colloquī: talk on the phone

    modern

  • accūsātīvus cum īnfīnītīvō: that

    classical

  • cum magnus eris: when you’re big

    classical

  • cum adolēveris: when you’re big

    classical

  • fūnis dēclīvis cum sēde mōbilī: zip line

    our formation

Examples

  • cum bene sit clausae caveā Pandīone nātae, nītitur in silvās illa redīre suās

    though Pandion’s daughter is well off shut in her cage, she strains to go back to her woodsOv. Pont. 1.3.39–40

    In the entry for although

  • quī cum ūnā domō jam capī nōn possint, in aliās domōs tamquam in colōniās exeunt

    since they can no longer fit in one house, they go out to other houses, as if to coloniesCic. Off. 1.54

    In the entry for since

  • cui Cossinius: quoniam satis bālāstī, inquit, ō Faustule noster

    to whom Cossinius said: “since you have bleated enough, our dear Faustulus”Varr. RR 2.3.1

    In the entry for since

  • dē pāvōnibus, inquit, līberē licet dīcās, quoniam discessit Fircellius

    “you may speak freely about peacocks,” he said, “now that Fircellius has gone”Varr. RR 3.6.1

    In the entry for since

  • Facile omnēs, cum valēmus, rēcta cōnsilia aegrōtīs damus.

    When we are well, we all find it easy to give good advice to the sick.Ter. And. 309

    In the entry for when

  • istō bonō ūtāre, dum adsit; cum absit, nē requīrās

    make use of that good while you have it; when it is gone, do not pine for itCic. Sen. 33

    In the entry for when

  • ut Cratēs, cum indoctum puerum vīdisset, paedagōgum ejus percussit

    as Crates, when he had seen an ignorant boy, struck the boy’s tutorQuint. 1.9.5

    In the entry for when

  • quem ubi vīdī, equidem vim lacrimārum prōfūdī

    when I saw him, I burst into tearsCic. Rep. 6.14 (Lewis & Short)

    In the entry for when

  • ut vēnī in Arpīnās, cum ad mē frāter vēnisset, in prīmīs nōbīs sermō isque multus dē tē fuit

    when I arrived at Arpinum and my brother had come to me, our first talk, and a long one, was about youCic. Att. 5.1.3

    In the entry for when

  • nōs Tusculānō ita dēlectāmur ut nōbīsmet ipsīs tum dēnique cum illō vēnimus placeāmus

    I love Tusculum so much that I only like myself when I get thereCic. Att. 1.6.2

    In the entry for whenever

  • cum aliī mālōs scandant, aliī per forōs cursent, aliī sentīnam exhauriant, ille autem clāvum tenēns quiētus sedeat in puppī

    while some climb the masts, others run along the gangways and others bail out the bilge, he sits quietly in the stern holding the tillerCic. Sen. 17

    In the entry for whereas

  • tempore illī praeceptō, at hī numerō avium rēgnum trahēbant

    the one side claimed the kingdom by being first, whereas the other claimed it by the number of birdsLiv. 1.7.1

    In the entry for whereas

  • vitiō vertunt, quia multa egeō; at ego illīs, quia nequeunt egēre

    they find fault with me because I go without many things, whereas I find fault with them because they cannot go withoutGell. 13.24.2

    In the entry for whereas

  • Sōcratēn ferunt, cum ūsque ad vesperum contentius ambulāret quaesītumque esset ex eō quārē id faceret, respondisse sē, quō melius cēnāret, obsōnāre ambulandō famem

    they say that Socrates, when he was walking hard till evening and was asked why, answered that he was buying in hunger by walking, so as to dine betterCic. Tusc. 5.97

    In the entry for while
